panels.rationale: Single axial brain MRI (FLAIR) of a human patient from a TTP-focused case article, with a white arrow marking a small cortical hyperintense lesion with restricted diffusion representing an acute infarction in the medial right frontal lobe. Cerebral microinfarction is a recognized neurologic manifestation of TTP, so the panel is included as a variant (single small acute infarct) presentation of thrombotic_thrombocytopenic_purpura.

in_text_mentions: nt, a CT scan brain was done to rule out meningitis, and it was unremarkable. However, due to the patient's continuing confusion and poor improvement in the level of consciousness, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained, and a small 1 cm area of the cortical hyperintense signal was detected at the mesial gyrus adjacent to the corpus callosum. This 1 cm area shows restricted diffusion and could represent an inflammatory process such as encephalitis. In addition, the MRI showed hyperintense focus in the white matter of the right occipital lobe, indicating a microhemorrhage (Figures 1, 2).

in_text_mentions: Despite undergoing plasmapheresis over five days, the patient’s anemia and thrombocytopenia showed no improvement. The ADAMTS13 level was within normal limits (Table 1). Given her persistent bicytopenia, a bone marrow biopsy was recommended. A repeat peripheral smear revealed similar findings as the initial evaluation, with the persistence of the thrombocytopenia, numerous schistocytes and fragmented red blood cells (RBCs), polychromasia, and nucleated RBCs with marked anisocytosis and poikilocytosis (Figures 1, 2).

Real patient image, adequately clear; arrow annotations present.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial DWI brain MRI of a real patient with a single arrow marking a punctate DWI-bright lesion in the right parietal lobe; caption and in-text explicitly attribute this to acute microvascular ischemic infarcts in the setting of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (article title specifies acquired TTP). Directly matches the configured TTP cerebral-microinfarctions finding; no diagram, control, or third-party issue. [raw subtype: acquired] B: Lower axial brain MRI slice of the same patient with two arrows indicating additional punctate right-parietal lesions. The caption attributes these to punctate acute infarcts/microvascular ischemia in TTP, and the article title specifies acquired TTP; matches the configured TTP cerebral-microinfarctions finding. Real patient imaging, no exclusion criterion met. [raw subtype: acquired]

Given the clinical history of our patient, who presented a single clinical exacerbation, and the MRI findings, which reported a single active lesion, we initiated the administration of beta-interferon-1a (Avonex) once per week. Following 9 months of weekly im injections, the patient was admitted after developing multiple bruises and ecchymosis on her limbs and torso, associated with epistaxis and gingival bleeding (Figure 1a,b). A few days before the onset of her symptomatology, the patient complained of a severe headache that was non-responsive to common analgesics (naproxen 220 mg).

he interferon treatment, the patient’s blood pressure and blood tests were monitored every 3 months, including complete blood count (CBC), liver enzymes and renal function, with no abnormal results. Moreover, she has had no clinical relapse since the initiation of Avonex. The initial diagnosis screening revealed severe thrombocytopenia (4000/mm3), increased WBC, lymphocytopenia and microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia with frequent schistocytes on the peripheral blood smear (Figure 1b). A brain and cervical spine MRI showed no active demyelinating lesions compared to the moment of MS diagnosis.

panels.figure_caption: Isolated periumbilical purpuric lesion associated with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. Clinical photograph demonstrating an isolated, non-blanching violaceous purpuric macule located in the left periumbilical region of the abdomen. The lesion is well-defined, non-palpable, and surrounded by normal-appearing skin, without evidence of necrosis, ulceration, or superimposed infection. The appearance is consistent with thrombocytopenia-related cutaneous bleeding in the setting of thrombotic microangiopathy secondary to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed two isolated cutaneous hemorrhagic lesions. Multiple discrete, non-blanching erythematous-to-violaceous petechial and purpuric lesions of varying size were present on the anterior aspect of the left thigh (Figure 1). In addition, a solitary, well-defined, non-palpable purpuric macule was observed in the left periumbilical region without evidence of necrosis, ulceration, or superimposed infection (Figure 2). Both lesions were consistent with thrombocytopenia-related cutaneous bleeding.

in_text_mentions: A peripheral blood smear was ordered, which showed 4% schistocytes (Figure 1) and large platelets. Her PLASMIC score was 7 (corresponding to a high probability of TTP), and a blood sample was sent for an urgent ADAMST13 level. In the meantime, the patient was started on 1000 mg of daily pulse steroids (methylprednisolone) for three days and therapeutic plasma exchange with 1.5 plasma volumes. After two sessions of plasma exchange on two consecutive days, her confusion resolved, and her platelet levels started to increase.

panels.rationale: Single-panel peripheral blood smear from a real patient. The caption and in-text text explicitly describe schistocytes (fragmented erythrocytes, including helmet-shaped forms marked by arrows) together with anisopoikilocytosis, in a patient whose presentation and management are attributed to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura in the article title and text; microangiopathic schistocytes are a textbook manifestation of TTP. The smear also shows sickle cells reflecting the patient's underlying sickle cell beta-thalassemia, which is a comorbidity rather than the manifestation being curated; it is noted only as a proposed finding. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text mentions (the article title says "Adult Patient" but age is not taken from the title per the field rules), and skin tone is not applicable to a blood smear.
panels.attribution_text: Shaik et al. Parvovirus Infection and Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura in an Adult Patient With Sickle Cell Beta-Thalassemia.. Cureus 2021. doi:10.7759/cureus.16173. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Peripheral smear showing schistocytes and anisopoikilocytosis
in_text_mentions: . Pregnancy-induced TTP was less likely due to its worsening with blood transfusion. This called for a multidisciplinary decision to stop the transfusion and continue expectant management with antipyretics, analgesics, and hydration. Peripheral smear on Day 5 showed microcytosis, hypochromia, polychromasia, and anisopoikilocytosis with schistocytes and sickle cells (Figures 1-2). Complete blood count (CBC), Coombs, and sickling test were again repeated daily. On Day 5, the sickling test and IDCT were positive and the reticulocyte count was 8%, which was a sign of improved bone marrow response.

panels.rationale: Single-panel clinical photograph of the left thigh of a TTP patient showing multiple discrete non-blanching erythematous-to-violaceous petechial and purpuric lesions, explicitly captioned and described in-text as cutaneous hemorrhagic manifestations of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura related to severe thrombocytopenia and microvascular injury. The visible small dark non-blanching spots on the hairy thigh skin are consistent with the captioned petechiae/purpura. No necrosis, ulceration, or bullae are present. Prior caption triage confirms a real patient image with no third-party restriction. Petechial/purpuric eruption is a classic cutaneous manifestation of TTP. Age and ethnicity are not stated; skin tone judged from the adequately visible, though dimly lit, skin as medium.
panels.attribution_text: Rodrigues et al. Severe Immune-Mediated Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura With High-Titer ADAMTS13 Inhibitors: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.112586. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Cutaneous hemorrhagic manifestations of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura involving the left thigh. Clinical photographs of the left thigh showing multiple discrete, non-blanching erythematous-to-violaceous petechial and purpuric lesions of varying size. A larger, well-circumscribed purpuric macule is seen adjacent to smaller petechiae. No evidence of skin necrosis, ulceration, bullae, or secondary infection is observed. These findings are consistent with cutaneous hemorrhagic manifestations associated with severe thrombocytopenia and microvascular injury in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.
in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed two isolated cutaneous hemorrhagic lesions. Multiple discrete, non-blanching erythematous-to-violaceous petechial and purpuric lesions of varying size were present on the anterior aspect of the left thigh (Figure 1). In addition, a solitary, well-defined, non-palpable purpuric macule was observed in the left periumbilical region without evidence of necrosis, ulceration, or superimposed infection (Figure 2). Both lesions were consistent with thrombocytopenia-related cutaneous bleeding.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Genuine diffusion-weighted brain MRI of a patient with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and severe thrombocytopenia (TTP-pentad context) showing an acute right corona radiata infarction (yellow arrow); the disease-focused article title and captioned manifestation support TTP cerebral microinfarction attribution, although the caption hedges that embolic/other thrombotic etiologies cannot be excluded, lowering confidence. B: Genuine diffusion-weighted brain MRI (companion slice) showing an acute left basal frontal cortical infarction (yellow arrow) in the same patient with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and severe thrombocytopenia; together with panel A this is multifocal bilateral cerebral ischemic injury fitting TTP cerebral microinfarctions, with the same caption hedge on embolic/other thrombotic etiologies.

panels.figure_caption: Diffusion-weighted MRI demonstrating acute bilateral frontal ischemic infarctions Brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging showing acute ischemic infarctions (arrows) involving (A) the right corona radiata and (B) the left basal frontal cortical region, with associated periventricular leukoencephalopathic changes and cortical atrophy. These lesions were temporally associated with the patient's transient neurological episodes in the setting of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia and severe thrombocytopenia; a mechanistic link to microvascular injury is plausible but cannot be established by imaging alone, and embolic or other thrombotic etiologies cannot be excluded.

panels.rationale: Real patient axial head CT showing a hypodense cerebral lesion consistent with ischemic stroke in a patient with idiopathic TTP, as confirmed by the article title and in-text description. The disease attribution is strong; the manifestation (cerebral infarction) is a recognized complication of TTP microvascular thrombosis. The vocabulary finding key is MRI-specific but represents the same pathological entity; a CT-specific finding is proposed.

panels.figure_caption: CT scan of the head: initial head CT scan on presentation and admission
in_text_mentions: A 40‐year‐old African female was referred to the Emergency on account of a stroke confirmed by a CT scan brought from the referring center (Figure 1). She presented with slurred speech, facial asymmetry, and left upper and lower limb weakness of 1‐day duration. The patient had been diagnosed with hypertension 10 years ago but had been noncompliant with her medication 2 weeks before her presentation. Her medications included amlodipine and lisinopril. panels.rationale: Single-panel real patient peripheral blood smear from a TTP-focused case report (Parvovirus Infection and Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura in an Adult Patient With Sickle Cell Beta-Thalassemia). The in-text explicitly states that the Day-5 smear (Figures 1-2) showed schistocytes, and schistocytes are a classic manifestation of TTP (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia), so the panel shows a configured-disease manifestation and is attributed to TTP. The smear also displays coexisting sickle-cell/thalassemia features (sickle cells, target cells, polychromasia) from the underlying hemoglobinopathy; these are noted as proposed findings only and do not drive the TTP attribution. Modality is 'other' because this is a Wright-Giemsa peripheral blood smear (hematology cytology), not an H&E tissue section, IHC, or immunofluorescence. No age or ethnicity is stated in the caption or in-text, so age_group is unknown and ethnicity is null. Confidence is moderate because schistocytes are supported by the in-text rather than the figure caption alone and the field is dominated by sickle-cell morphology.

in_text_mentions: . Pregnancy-induced TTP was less likely due to its worsening with blood transfusion. This called for a multidisciplinary decision to stop the transfusion and continue expectant management with antipyretics, analgesics, and hydration. Peripheral smear on Day 5 showed microcytosis, hypochromia, polychromasia, and anisopoikilocytosis with schistocytes and sickle cells (Figures 1-2). Complete blood count (CBC), Coombs, and sickling test were again repeated daily. On Day 5, the sickling test and IDCT were positive and the reticulocyte count was 8%, which was a sign of improved bone marrow response.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 8 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H). A: Gross postmortem specimen of the heart from a confirmed TTP case showing many petechial hemorrhagic lesions in the right ventricle wall (arrowheads), a macroscopic manifestation of TTP microvascular thrombosis. Cardiac involvement is a recognized but less common site, hence variant. No skin vocabulary entry matches myocardium, so the finding is proposed. B: HE histology of myocardium from the TTP case showing microthrombi in small blood vessels — the textbook histologic hallmark of TTP — with focal surrounding hemorrhage. C: Fibrin immunostain of the cardiac microthrombi showing only slight fibrin positivity, supporting the fibrin-poor, platelet-rich nature characteristic of TTP microthrombi. D: VWF immunostain showing markedly VWF-positive cardiac microthrombi — the classic ultrastructural signature of TTP (platelet-VWF-rich thrombi). E: HE histology of brain from the same TTP case showing occlusive microthrombi, the...

plate_findings.evidence: Axial diffusion-weighted imaging reveals focal diffusion restriction in the left cerebellum (arrows); in-text: acute multiple punctate infarcts in bilateral basal ganglia, thalami, frontal lobes, and cerebellum

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial DWI MRI showing a focal diffusion-restricted punctate infarct in the left cerebellum in a fulminant TTP patient; article title and caption directly attribute the multiterritorial punctate infarcts to TTP. B: ADC map confirming true restricted diffusion of the cerebellar punctate infarct, a classic MRI correlate of acute cerebral microinfarction in TTP. C: DWI showing bilateral deep gray matter punctate infarcts, a recognized classic MRI pattern of multiterritorial cerebral microinfarction in TTP. D: DWI showing a frontal lobe punctate infarct completing the multiterritorial acute ischemic pattern described in the caption and attributed to TTP in the article title.

panels.figure_caption: Brain MRI showed numerous acute punctate infarcts consistent with a multiterritorial ischemic stroke. Axial diffusion-weighted imaging (A) reveals focal diffusion restriction in the left cerebellum (arrows), confirmed by true restricted diffusion on the corresponding ADC map (B). Additional DWI images demonstrate infarcts in the basal ganglia and thalami (C), as well as the frontal lobes (D). ADC: Apparent diffusion coefficient, DWI: Diffusion-weighted imaging
in_text_mentions: s methylprednisolone. Despite therapy, she developed a generalized tonic-clonic seizure on day three and was started on levetiracetam and lacosamide. The patient became obtunded following the seizures and was intubated for airway protection. Brain MRI revealed acute multiple punctate infarcts in bilateral basal ganglia, thalami, frontal lobes, and cerebellum (Figure 2). Rituximab was initiated on hospital day four. Over the next several days, her platelet count remained critically low, and additional immunosuppressive therapy with IV cyclophosphamide was initiated. Caplacizumab was also added.

panels.rationale: Single-panel peripheral blood smear from a real patient with acquired TTP (article title: acquired TTP following Pfizer COVID-19 vaccination). The caption and in-text state the smear shows schistocytes (>8 per high power field), and the image visibly shows fragmented red cells (helmet/triangular schistocytes) among erythrocytes. Schistocytes on peripheral smear are a textbook manifestation of TTP, directly matching the configured vocabulary finding. No annotations, no third-party copyright, no other disease shown. [raw subtype: acquired]

The caption and in-text explicitly state 8-10% schistocytes suggesting TTP, and the image visibly shows fragmented erythrocytes (schistocytes/helmet cells) alongside a neutrophil and red cells with anisopoikilocytosis. Fibrinogen level, prothrombin time/international normalized ratio (INR), and partial thromboplastin time were within normal limits. panels.rationale: Single-panel figure: a real patient peripheral blood smear (cytology, Wright-Giemsa type preparation, hence modality 'other' rather than histology_he) from a case report titled 'Furosemide-Induced Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura: A Report of a Rare Case.' The caption and in-text state the smear revealed schistocytes with few platelets, and the image visibly shows fragmented red blood cells (schistocytes, indicated by black arrows) together with a neutrophil and sparse platelets. Schistocytes with thrombocytopenia in this disease-focused context is a classic, specific manifestation of TTP, so the panel is included with the schistocytes finding tagged to thrombotic_thrombocytopenic_purpura.

in_text_mentions: Initial laboratory investigations on admission (Table 1) were significant for anemia, thrombocytopenia, high lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), low serum haptoglobin, and an increased reticulocyte count. A peripheral smear revealed schistocytes with few platelets (Figure 4). Serum creatinine was within normal limits. The direct antibody test was negative. Chest roentgenogram and computed tomography of the head and facial bones were unremarkable.

in_text_mentions: He was managed with plasma exchange therapy, intravenous methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg daily, followed by weekly rituximab. He was continued on insulin, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and supportive care for DKA. His clinical course was complicated by worsening renal function (Figure 1). His platelet count and Hb levels continued to remain low despite plasmapheresis. On day six, he developed seizures, followed by lower limb weakness. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed diffuse white matter abnormalities and multiple small punctate hemorrhages (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: Suspected of having a stroke based on the symptoms of her neurological disorder, a brain MRI was requested. Brain MRI (without gadolinium) reported multiple acute infarction areas in the left temporoparietal, right temporofrontal, and right parietal cortex (fig 1). According to creatinine rise with thrombocytopenia and brain infarction along with hematuria and proteinuria, a kidney needle biopsy (KNB) was asked. The KNB reported glomerular changes like membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) with obliterated small arteries consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy (fig 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial DWI from a real patient brain MRI in a case report of TTP presenting with ischemic stroke; shows restricted diffusion in the right parietotemporal region, consistent with subacute infarction from TTP microvascular occlusion — the classic MRI correlate of TTP neurological involvement. B: Axial FLAIR image from the same TTP patient MRI showing a hyperintense subacute infarct in the right parietotemporal region, corroborating multifocal cerebral infarction as a manifestation of thrombotic microangiopathy. C: Axial T1-weighted image from the same TTP patient MRI completing the described multifocal subacute infarction set; lesion signal is less conspicuous on T1, slightly lowering confidence relative to DWI/FLAIR, but the panel is clearly part of the same diagnostic MRI study in a TTP case.

in_text_mentions: pileptiform discharges. The differential diagnosis for this seizure was an ischemic stroke or generalized tonic-clonic seizure induced by TTP. A T2-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with and without contrast, in addition to a magnetic resonance venography (MRV), revealed subacute right frontal and acute cerebellar lacunar infarcts, confirming that the patient had a stroke (Figure 1). panels.rationale: Single-panel peripheral blood smear at 1,000x from a real patient showing fragmented red cells (schistocytes, including a helmet/triangular fragment) and a multi-lobed hypersegmented neutrophil. Schistocytes are the textbook microangiopathic-hemolysis manifestation of TTP, and the prior caption triage routed this figure as keep for TTP. Attribution is moderated because the article is a mimic case report: the pancytopenic presentation with schistocytosis was suspected TTP but ultimately attributed to metformin-induced cobalamin deficiency, so the image captures a TTP-like smear rather than a confirmed TTP case; confidence reflects this ambiguity. The hypersegmented neutrophil (a cobalamin-deficiency feature absent from the vocabulary) is recorded as a proposed finding. No age or ethnicity stated in the provided text; not a skin panel.

in_text_mentions: Suspected of having a stroke based on the symptoms of her neurological disorder, a brain MRI was requested. Brain MRI (without gadolinium) reported multiple acute infarction areas in the left temporoparietal, right temporofrontal, and right parietal cortex (fig 1). According to creatinine rise with thrombocytopenia and brain infarction along with hematuria and proteinuria, a kidney needle biopsy (KNB) was asked. The KNB reported glomerular changes like membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) with obliterated small arteries consistent with thrombotic microangiopathy (fig 2).

panels.rationale: Single-panel clinical photograph of a real patient showing a crusted bloody lesion at the entrance of the right nostril. The article title and in-text context identify the patient as having furosemide-induced thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and the lesion represents nasal mucosal hemorrhage, a hemorrhagic manifestation of TTP-related thrombocytopenia. The manifestation is a recognized but less prominent hemorrhagic sign (variant rather than the classic extensive petechial-purpuric eruption). No age or ethnicity is stated; skin appears light-toned though the image has a warm color cast.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real patient brain MRI from a disease-focused TTP article; DWI shows focal left MCA-territory diffusion restriction with multifocal infarcts, a cerebral thrombotic manifestation of TTP. B: ADC map corroborates acute infarcts rather than T2 shine-through; in the TTP-focused case this supports cerebral thrombotic ischemic injury. C: Multifocal scattered diffusion-restricted small cerebral infarcts on DWI are a recognized MRI manifestation of TTP in the disease-focused article. D: Follow-up DWI shows bilateral multifocal small infarcts consistent with TTP cerebral microinfarctions; mass effect is noted by caption in this fulminant case.
